clue.text: Hardest areas after storm revealing place with water shortage

indicators.note: after a storm things are tossed about, so the letters of the two words lie in a new order

explanation.surface: Arid regions, battered by a storm, reveal a spot where water is scarce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardest areas' is the fodder in full: all twelve letters are rearranged, and 'revealing' only links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The great North African desert is the classic example of a region lacking rainfall.

clue.text: Porn supremo perhaps becoming less successful

parts.note: pornography is a sin to the moralist, so the word gives sin
a supremo is the top figure, a king of the field

explanation.surface: A pornography baron is pictured, perhaps as an empire in decline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' flags that a porn supremo is one fanciful example of a king of sin.
explanation.definitionFit: A business or ship that is sinking is going downhill, failing steadily.

clue.text: Willing to participate, gave out in a ring after heavyweight's entrance

indicators.note: after places the rest following the heavyweight's opening letter
the entrance of a word is its opening letter, here the heavyweight's
in sets the rearranged letters between the a and the ring

parts.note: a ring is round like the letter O

indicators.note: out suggests the letters of gave are thrown out of order

explanation.surface: A boxer gave up in the ring once the heavyweight came in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' makes the anagram VEAG; 'in' sits it inside A and O, and 'entrance' gives H, which 'after' puts first.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a go is to make an attempt, so the hyphenated adjective describes someone game to try.

clue.text: Artists risk altering top of traditional mini?

parts.note: an RA is a Royal Academician, so two artists give RA twice

indicators.note: altering changes the order of the letters of the word risk
the top of a word is its first letter, here of traditional

explanation.surface: Artists take a gamble by updating a traditional piece of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'altering' turns RISK into SKIR. RA (Royal Academician) is the crossword shorthand for an artist.
explanation.definitionFit: The ra-ra skirt is a short flounced style, so it is one example of a mini, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Look defeated — day turning not so good

indicators.note: turning means the word for not so good is read backwards

parts.note: poor means not so good, of low quality

explanation.surface: Someone looks beaten as a day goes from bad to worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' gives ROOP.
explanation.definitionFit: To droop is to sag or hang down in dejection, the posture of someone downcast.

clue.text: Sea still not quite stormy? Be on your way

indicators.note: a stormy sea is churned up, so these letters are thrown into a new order
not quite means the word still loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A sailor wonders whether calm water is turning rough enough to depart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' trims STILL to STIL; 'stormy' then rearranges SEA plus STIL.
explanation.definitionFit: To set sail is to begin a voyage, and by extension to depart on any journey.

clue.text: Recipe: various ingredients to make in small baking dish

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for recipe, from Latin recipe, take

indicators.note: various ingredients suggests the letters are mixed into a different combination

explanation.surface: A recipe lists assorted ingredients to cook in a little oven dish.
explanation.walkthrough: R for recipe is the traditional prescription symbol. 'various ingredients' rearranges MAKE IN to AMEKIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A ramekin is a small individual ceramic pot for baking souffles and similar dishes.

clue.text: You and the congregation receiving start of sermon many times over

indicators.note: receiving means the pieces take a letter in among them

parts.note: thou is the old form of you
a fold is a flock, so a church congregation

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, here of sermon

explanation.surface: A preacher addresses the listener and the flock as the sermon begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'receiving' takes S ('start of sermon') in. A fold, a sheep pen, is a common image for a church congregation, its flock.
explanation.definitionFit: Thousandfold means multiplied by a thousand, so a huge number of times.

clue.text: European city exchange disregarding Germany?

indicators.note: disregarding means the letter for Germany is left out

parts.note: a handover is a transfer or exchange
D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: A query whether a trade can go ahead without German involvement.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is fair: the city itself is German, so the surface is ironic.
explanation.definitionFit: Hanover is a major city in northern Germany, capital of Lower Saxony.

clue.text: Agree to take part with mother withholding name? That's for the best

indicators.note: withholding means the letter for name is kept back, taken out of the agreeing phrase

parts.note: to opt in is to agree to participate
mum is mother

explanation.surface: Someone joins in with their mother but keeps their identity secret, all for the best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'withholding' drops N from OPTIN, leaving OPTI.
explanation.definitionFit: The optimum is the most favourable condition or the ideal option.

clue.text: Unemotional mother not fancying performance containing minimum of theatricality

indicators.note: containing means the pieces hold a letter within them

parts.note: mater is Latin for mother, used jokingly in English

indicators.note: the minimum of a word is its smallest part, its first letter

parts.note: to be off something is to have lost one's liking for it
an act is a performance on stage

explanation.surface: A mother with no taste for drama sits through a show with little theatricality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'containing' takes in T ('minimum of theatricality'). Mater for mother is old public-school slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter-of-fact manner is plain and practical, showing no feeling.

clue.text: Mountain range contains popular places to go

indicators.note: contains means the range wraps around another word

parts.note: the Urals are the range dividing Europe and Asia
in means popular, fashionable

explanation.surface: A mountain range is said to hold well-liked destinations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'places to go' reads like holiday spots, but 'go' is the euphemism for relieving oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: Going to the loo is a euphemism, so urinals are literally places where men go.

clue.text: Something missing in favourite feature of skirt

indicators.note: in means the missing thing goes inside the favourite

parts.note: a pet is a favourite
a lack is an absence, something missing

explanation.surface: Something is absent from a much-loved part of a skirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A placket is the slit opening in a skirt or dress for fastenings.

clue.text: Intimidating behaviour in the past involving historic monarch

indicators.note: involving means the past phrase wraps around the monarch

parts.note: ago means in the past
GR is George Rex, King George's cipher

explanation.surface: Bullying in olden days centred on a long-dead king.
explanation.walkthrough: GR (Georgius Rex) is the royal cipher of the Georgian kings, seen on old postboxes.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggro is British slang for aggressive, threatening conduct or trouble.

clue.text: The writer's weapon to constrain junior academic bias

indicators.note: to constrain means the pieces hold another inside them

parts.note: the writer is the setter, so the writer's (is) gives I'm
a lance is a long spear
a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is the lowest degree holder

explanation.surface: An author uses a sword of words to rein in a prejudiced young lecturer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to constrain' has the pieces enclose the junior academic. 'The writer' is the setter, so 'The writer's' is I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: An imbalance is a lack of even proportion, a skew in one direction.

clue.text: Run from sponsor cornering male in part of theatre

indicators.note: cornering means the trimmed word traps another inside
from means the letter for run is taken away

parts.note: a backer is a sponsor
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
a stag is a male deer

explanation.surface: A man flees a sponsor who has him trapped in the wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run from' leaves BACKE, which 'cornering' wraps around the male.
explanation.definitionFit: Backstage is the area behind the stage, out of the audience's view.

clue.text: Name put down, after reflection, to receive college discourse

indicators.note: to receive means the reversed words take in a letter
after reflection means the words are mirrored, read backwards

parts.note: to cite is to name or mention
laid means put down

explanation.surface: A name is written down, and after thought a university discussion follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after reflection' gives DIALETIC; 'to receive' takes in C.
explanation.definitionFit: Dialectic is reasoned argument or debate in search of truth.

clue.text: Opposed to information describing component of vaccine

parts.note: anti means against, opposed to
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: An anti-vaccine view is offered about what goes into a jab.
explanation.definitionFit: An antigen is the substance that prompts an immune response, which vaccines contain.

clue.text: Bean, cheese and meat — not good

parts.note: Edam is a Dutch cheese

indicators.note: not means the letter for good is removed

parts.note: game is wild meat such as venison

explanation.surface: A menu lists beans, cheese and meat, but the meat is bad.
explanation.definitionFit: Edamame are immature soybeans, served in the pod.

clue.text: Rat in middle of pigeonry? That's an inspiration

indicators.note: in means the rat sits inside those central letters
the middle of a word is its central letters, here of pigeonry

explanation.surface: A rat has got into the dovecote, and that sparks an idea.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle of an eight-letter word is its central pair, here the fourth and fifth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Muse of lyric poetry, and Muses are the classical sources of artistic inspiration.

clue.text: Composer dismissing a writer and painter

indicators.note: dismissing means the letter a is sent away

parts.note: Edward Elgar was an English composer
Umberto Eco was an Italian novelist

explanation.surface: A composer sacks a writer and a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dismissing a' takes A out of ELGAR, leaving ELGR.
explanation.definitionFit: El Greco was the Cretan-born Spanish Renaissance painter.

clue.text: Religious traveller embedding stone in a staff

indicators.note: embedding means the stone is set within the other pieces

parts.note: a pole is a staff or stick
ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight

explanation.surface: A pilgrim fixes a stone into a walking staff.
explanation.walkthrough: ST is a stone, a British unit of weight of fourteen pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostle is a missionary who travels to spread the faith.

clue.text: Biscuit: a form of tack consumed by Old English

indicators.note: consumed by means the rearranged letters are swallowed inside another piece
a form of means the letters of tack take a different shape

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned ship's biscuit was eaten by early English folk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form of' rearranges TACK to TCAK. Tack, or hardtack, is a sailor's hard biscuit, which keeps the surface in the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: An oatcake is a flat, savoury oatmeal cracker, often Scottish.

clue.text: Upright before going to court

parts.note: ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A litigant stands straight before going into the courtroom.
explanation.definitionFit: Erect means standing straight, vertical.

clue.text: Agree to start work?

parts.note: approving a project formally lets it begin, though the phrase usually means finishing work

explanation.surface: A query whether to approve beginning a job.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase also means to end a shift or broadcast, the opposite of starting, which is the joke behind the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: To sign off on a plan is to give formal approval so it can proceed.

clue.text: Diminish qualification somewhat diminished after receiving commercial endorsement?

indicators.note: after receiving means the shortened word takes another piece inside
somewhat diminished means the word loses a little, its final letter

parts.note: a degree is an academic qualification
an ad is a commercial, a paid promotion

explanation.surface: A degree loses value once it has been plugged in an advert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somewhat diminished' leaves DEGRE, which 'after receiving' opens to take the advert.
explanation.definitionFit: To degrade something is to lower it in quality or worth.

clue.text: Clean and healthy account about start of month

indicators.note: about means the account letters wrap around another piece

parts.note: Sept I reads as the first of September, the start of a month

explanation.surface: A sound financial statement is drawn up at the beginning of a month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start of month' is not the letter M: it is SEPT I, 1 September written with a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Aseptic means free from germs, sterile and so hygienic.

clue.text: Where horse manure may go, confidentially

definitions.meaning: gardeners spread manure beneath rose bushes, literally below the plant
in secret, from the rose as an old symbol of secrecy

explanation.surface: A gardener discreetly says where to put the dung.
explanation.definitionFit: Sub rosa, its Latin form, means privately; a rose hung over a meeting once marked it secret.
